items.paragraph: Projects that recruit volunteers to count birds, record flowering dates or photograph insects are often dismissed by professional researchers on the grounds that amateurs make mistakes. The objection is true and largely beside the point. Individual records from volunteers are indeed less reliable than those of trained surveyors, but the errors tend to be random rather than systematic, and random errors shrink in importance as the number of observations grows. A thousand imperfect counts spread across a region can reveal a trend that a handful of expert surveys, confined to a few accessible sites, would miss altogether. The real weakness of such data lies elsewhere: volunteers go where it is pleasant to go, at weekends and in good weather, so the gaps in their coverage are anything but random. The question to ask of citizen science is therefore not how careful each participant is but where and when the participants chose to look.

items.paragraph: Of the writing produced in the ancient world, only a fraction survives, and it is natural to suppose that what remains is the best of it, the works later readers judged worth preserving. There is some truth in this: texts that nobody valued were seldom recopied, and a text not recopied every few generations was likely to perish with its material. But value to later copyists is not the same as quality. Works survived when they suited the needs of schools and religious communities, when they were short enough to copy cheaply, or when they had been gathered into anthologies that travelled together; a brilliant treatise in an unfashionable field could vanish while a mediocre school text was copied hundreds of times. The surviving corpus is a record of what later centuries used, and our sense of what the ancients thought best is partly an inheritance of those uses.

items.paragraph: Two strategies compete for the limited money available to protect plant diversity. Seed banks store frozen samples of thousands of species in secure vaults, offering insurance against extinction at modest cost. Conservation in the wild protects plants where they grow, along with the insects, fungi and soils they depend on. The seed bank's great advantage is security, but its samples are frozen in time: a population kept in a vault stops adapting to changing climate and pests, and some species have seeds that cannot survive drying and freezing at all. Wild populations go on evolving, but they are exposed to every threat the vault avoids. Neither strategy can substitute for the other. The vault is best understood as a backup for living populations, not a replacement for them.

items.paragraph: National income accounts leave out the cooking, cleaning and care done unpaid within households, and the omission is often called a simple bias that a better statistic would correct. The criticism is right that something valuable goes unmeasured, and that this can distort judgements: when a family starts paying for childcare it once provided itself, measured output rises though little more care may be given. But the remedy is less simple than it sounds. To add household work to the accounts one must price it, and every method of pricing an hour of unpaid care, whether at what a hired carer would earn or at what the carer could have earned elsewhere, imposes a market valuation on activity whose meaning to those who do it is often precisely that it is not done for money. The omission is a real flaw, but the obvious fix may trade one distortion for another.

items.paragraph: After spilling coffee on a shirt or stumbling over a word in a meeting, people often feel that everyone noticed and will remember. Usually few did. This overestimate, sometimes called the spotlight effect, arises because each of us experiences our own appearance and actions from the inside, vividly and continuously, and we find it hard to adjust for the fact that others are busy with their own concerns. items.paragraph: Conservation has traditionally worked from a picture: a meadow, a heath or a wetland as it looked at some chosen date, to be kept that way by mowing, burning and weeding. Rewilding with large herbivores starts from a different premise. Instead of fixing a picture, it reintroduces grazing animals such as cattle, horses or bison, or their nearest modern stand-ins, and lets their feeding, trampling and wallowing decide what the land becomes. Critics point out that the results cannot be specified in advance, and that a project unable to say what it is aiming at is hard to fund, monitor or defend. (4) None of this makes rewilding suitable everywhere; a small reserve protecting one rare orchid may need exactly the kind of fixed management that rewilding rejects.

items.paragraph: Economists tend to defend surge pricing on grounds of efficiency: when demand for rides or rooms spikes, a higher price rations the scarce supply to those who value it most and draws more suppliers in. The reasoning holds within its own terms, but it explains less of the public reaction than its defenders suppose. People who resent a tripled fare during a storm are not usually confused about supply and demand; they are objecting to what the price seems to say, that a seller is profiting from their predicament. Norms of fairness in many communities treat raising prices in an emergency differently from raising them on a busy Saturday, even when the economics are identical. A pricing scheme that ignores this distinction may be efficient on paper and still erode the goodwill on which the seller depends.

items.paragraph: Detailed marking rubrics are usually defended as a protection for students: they make expectations explicit, reduce the influence of a marker's mood and allow two examiners to reach the same grade. These are real gains, especially for routine tasks. The trouble begins when the same apparatus is applied to work whose value lies in doing something unexpected. A rubric can list only the qualities its authors anticipated, and a student who learns to satisfy each line, an introduction here, three examples there, is rewarded for matching the template rather than for thinking. An essay that takes an original route may score worse than a dutiful one because its strengths fall between the boxes. Consistency is worth having, but a scheme that is perfectly consistent about the wrong things is not fair; it is reliably unfair.

items.paragraph: When offices relax their dress codes, the change is usually welcomed as a move towards equality: without suits and ties, the argument goes, the junior clerk and the senior partner look alike, and people are judged by their work rather than their clothes. A formal rule could be learned once and followed by anyone who could afford a suit; the new norms, which separate the right kind of casual from the wrong kind, are rarely written down and are absorbed mostly by those already at home in the social world that sets them. items.paragraph: We defer to experts on bridges and medicines without hesitation, yet many people feel that deferring to someone else on a moral question (adopting a view on the ethics of eating meat simply because a thoughtful philosopher holds it) would be a failing. items.paragraph: Audiences who grow up with subtitled foreign films often regard dubbing as a betrayal: the actor's voice, half the performance, is replaced by a stranger's. Audiences raised on dubbing reply that subtitles betray the image instead, since the viewer's eyes spend much of each scene at the bottom of the frame and miss faces, gestures and composition. Each side is right about what the other loses and quiet about what its own method loses. Subtitles preserve the sound of a performance but condense its words, often dropping a good deal of the dialogue to suit the reading speed of viewers; dubbing keeps more of the dialogue and the whole image but sacrifices the voice. Neither is a transparent window onto the original. The choice is between two different losses, and preferring one is a judgement about which part of a film matters most, not a recognition that one method is faithful and the other is not.

items.paragraph: Arguments over renaming streets usually set two camps against each other. One holds that a name is a standing honour, and that keeping the name of someone whose deeds a city now condemns means continuing to honour them. The other holds that names are part of the historical record, and that erasing them tidies away an uncomfortable past. Both treat the name as if it had a single fixed meaning. In practice a street name works mostly as an address; few residents know whom their street commemorates, and the honour, if any, is faint. That faintness cuts both ways. It weakens the claim that the old name actively glorifies anyone, but it equally weakens the claim that removing it destroys history, which survives in archives and books rather than on signposts. The dispute is better seen as a contest over what a city chooses to say now than as a battle over the past.

items.paragraph: When an old dam is taken down, people often expect the river to return at once to the condition it was in before the dam was built. What usually happens is messier. Sediment that piled up behind the wall for decades is released and travels downstream, burying gravel beds and clouding the water for a season or more. Fish that had been blocked may take years to recolonise the upstream reaches, and the plants that first cover the drained reservoir bed are often weeds rather than the species that grew there before. None of this means that removal fails; on many rivers the long-term gains in fish passage and natural flow are substantial. It means that removal starts a process of recovery rather than restoring a finished state, and that the early years can look worse than what came before.

items.paragraph: Much of what is believed about diet and health rests on asking people what they eat. The objection usually raised against such surveys is that people forget, and forgetting, being random, merely adds noise. The deeper difficulty is that the errors are not random. People tend to under-report foods they regard as unhealthy and over-report those they think virtuous, and the size of the distortion varies with body weight, with education and with how much a person cares about appearing healthy. Since those same characteristics are themselves linked to health, the error can manufacture associations or hide real ones, rather than simply blurring them. This does not make dietary surveys useless; for some questions they are the only practical source. But it means that a large sample, which cures random error, offers no protection against this kind.

items.paragraph: Lavish weddings are often criticised as a simple failure of prudence: families spend their savings, or borrow, for a single day that leaves nothing behind. The criticism misreads what the money buys. In many communities a wedding is the occasion on which a family displays its standing to a wide network of relatives, neighbours and future in-laws, and that standing affects the marriages its other children can make, the help it can call on and the credit it is offered. Seen this way, the spending is less a lapse than an investment in reputation. None of this makes it harmless. When every family must match its neighbours, the display that once signalled standing becomes a cost that all must pay merely to avoid falling behind, and the people least able to afford it are pressed hardest.

items.paragraph: Many people feel that there is a sharp moral line between telling a lie and merely misleading someone with statements that are literally true. (1) In such cases the speaker has said nothing false, yet the listener is left with exactly the belief that a lie would have produced. Defenders of the distinction argue that the misleader at least leaves the listener a chance to notice the gap and ask a sharper question. (2) There is something to this, since a careful listener can sometimes detect an evasive answer where a lie would give no warning. (3) But the chance is often slight, and a speaker who chooses words precisely to avoid detection can hardly claim credit for the escape route he has hidden. The line between lying and misleading may matter for law and for manners, but morally it is far thinner than it feels. (4)
